subtype: Approach: writing down key points as a script [Action]
passage: Coach's note. Uday brought a difficult conversation to today's session: telling his team lead that he will leave in two months to study. He froze twice in earlier attempts, so we worked on structure. On a card he wrote four lines: thank you for the last three years, I have decided to go, the two reasons, and what I'd ask in return, a good handover period and a reference. I did not want him to read it aloud, and he agreed to keep it in his pocket. When we practised, he glanced at the card once and then spoke in his own words. Afterwards he said the card felt like a handrail. I suggested he pick a private moment. I will ask next week how it went. - Vandana

qa.q: What four lines did Uday write on his card?
qa.a: Thank you for the last three years, I have decided to go, the two reasons, and what I'd ask in return.

qa.q: What does Uday's remark that the card felt like a handrail suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests Uday feels nervous but steadied, with the card giving support without controlling his words.

qa.q: What could Uday do if he freezes again during the real talk?
qa.a: Uday could take a breath, glance at the card, or ask to continue after a short pause, and then speak in his own words.

qa.q: How might the team lead feel hearing the plan?
qa.a: The team lead may be surprised but likely respects the thanks and the clear, fair request.

grounding: Uday writes a short outline of thanks, the decision, the reasons and what he asks in return, which keeps him from freezing.

subtype: Approach: putting it off until the last moment [Pitfall]
passage: I kept waiting for the right moment to tell my parents about the job in Toronto, and the right moment never came. On every Sunday call I opened my mouth and asked about the neighbours instead. Then, three weeks before my visa interview, my aunt phoned Amma. "Ganga is going abroad, didn't she tell you?" Amma called me that night and her voice was quiet. "Why did I hear it from Bua?" I tried to say I had been protecting them. It sounded thin. It was not the moving that hurt; it was the finding out. It took Papa two days to speak to me. I think if I had told them in March, they would have cried and then helped me pack. Instead I had to earn back something I had not known I could lose. - Ganga

qa.q: Who told Amma about the job abroad?
qa.a: Ganga's aunt, Bua, phoned Amma and told her.

qa.q: What was Amma feeling when she asked "Why did I hear it from Bua?"
qa.a: Amma felt hurt and shut out, and her voice was quiet.

qa.q: What could Ganga do now to repair things?
qa.a: Ganga could apologise sincerely for not telling them, share the plans and a visiting schedule, and listen to their worries.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt during the two days before he spoke?
qa.a: Papa may have felt hurt and disappointed, taking time to gather himself before talking.

grounding: Ganga delays telling the parents about moving abroad until a relative does, and the way they learn hurts trust more than the decision.

passage: It started with a burnt dosa. My mother said, "You never watch the stove," and something in me snapped. I told her I was sick of the comments on my flat, my job, my friends, and the way she told Himani, my wife, what to buy. Then I said she had ruined our first year of marriage. My father stood up. Words came out that I cannot take back. The thing I had meant to ask, that they call before visiting, never got said. By evening nobody was speaking, and the only thing anyone remembered was the last sentence I shouted. I have thought about it many times: I had a fair request, and I buried it under years of complaints. - Vikram

qa.q: What did the quarrel start with?
qa.a: It started with a burnt dosa.

qa.q: What was Vikram feeling underneath the outburst?
qa.a: Vikram was feeling built-up frustration from years of comments, which came out all at once.

qa.q: What could Vikram do now?
qa.a: Vikram could apologise for the shouting and later ask calmly, on its own, for the parents to call before visiting.

qa.q: How might Vikram's mother have felt when the request got lost?
qa.a: Vikram's mother may have felt hurt and confused, since the only thing that came through was the anger.

grounding: After a small quarrel Vikram blurts out a long-held complaint about the parents' interference, and the real request gets lost.

subtype: Approach: over-rehearsing until it sounds scripted [Pitfall]
passage: For a week, Damini walked to the water tank behind the old bus stand in the kasba and said her lines to the wall: "Amma, I have accepted a teaching job at Pema's school in the next town. I will come home on Sundays. I have thought about it carefully." She knew each word. On Saturday night at the kitchen door, she said the first line. Her mother, kneading dough, did not look up. "Who will look after you there?" Damini's next line was about the salary. "That's not what I asked," said her mother. Damini said the line about Sundays. Her mother's hands slowed. Damini went on to her third line as if nothing had been said, and her mother went quiet and finished the dough. Later Damini saw that one roti had been left raw. She had never seen her mother leave anything raw.

qa.q: Where did Damini practise her lines?
qa.a: Damini practised at the water tank behind the old bus stand.

qa.q: What was Damini's mother really worried about, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was worried about who would look after Damini in the next town, shown by her question and the roti left raw.

qa.q: What could Damini do differently?
qa.a: Damini could put the script aside and answer the worry directly, by talking about where she will stay and who she will know there.

qa.q: How might Damini's mother have felt when Damini kept to the script?
qa.a: Damini's mother may have felt unheard and anxious, going quiet instead of asking again.

grounding: Damini memorises exact lines, sticks to them when her mother answers differently, and misses her mother's real worry.

subtype: Approach: sleeping on it and planning a follow-up talk [Revision]
passage: By nine, Sameer and Uma were talking over each other about whether Sameer's mother should move in with them. Voices rose. Uma stood at the sink, gripping a plate. Sameer felt his jaw tighten and heard himself say something sharp. He stopped. "This is going badly. Let's stop and pick it up tomorrow evening, after dinner." Uma looked at him for a long moment, then nodded. Nothing more was said that night; they watched an old film side by side, not touching. The next evening, tea in hand, they began again, more quietly. Uma said what she was afraid of: losing the quiet of the flat. Sameer said what he was afraid of: not being there for his mother. By ten they had a plan of three months, with a review at the end. Neither felt they had won.

qa.q: When did Sameer and Uma agree to continue the talk?
qa.a: The next evening, after dinner.

qa.q: What was Uma afraid of?
qa.a: Uma was afraid of losing the quiet of the flat.

qa.q: What could they do if the second talk also gets heated?
qa.a: They could pause again and carry on another day, since a hard conversation can be split across several days.

qa.q: How might Sameer's mother feel about the plan?
qa.a: Sameer's mother may feel relieved to be wanted, and perhaps a little worried about being a burden.

grounding: When the first talk becomes heated, Sameer says to continue tomorrow, and the calmer second talk reaches a plan.

subtype: Approach: asking a trusted friend or counsellor to help prepare [Action]
passage: I had my speech ready to tell Amma and Papa about the design course in Bengaluru. Before saying it, I tried it out on my friend Pankaj over chai. "What do your parents fear?" Pankaj asked. I laughed. "Nothing. They'll just be sad." "Are you sure?" I thought about it all the way home. Amma always said cities are lonely. Papa worried about who would look after me if I fell ill. I had never thought about either. I added a new line: "I'll come home every second month, and you can call me any evening." When I told them on Sunday, Amma's shoulders came down, and Papa asked about the hostel. It was not easy, but it was a conversation, not a quarrel. - Usha

qa.q: In which city is the design course?
qa.a: The design course is in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What did Usha realise about the parents' feelings after talking with Pankaj?
qa.a: Usha realised they were probably worried, Amma about loneliness and Papa about who would look after Usha if ill.

qa.q: What else could Usha do to ease the parents' worries?
qa.a: Usha could share the hostel details and a contact person there, so the parents can picture where Usha will be.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Usha promised to come home every second month?
qa.a: Amma may have felt relieved and reassured, as the shoulders coming down suggests.

grounding: Usha talks the plan through with a friend who asks what the parents fear, and adds a reassurance about visits to the message.

subtype: Approach: working backward from months of cash left [Thinking]
passage: Gurpreet had savings for nine months. On the wall of the rented room in Pune he drew a line: last salary in March, savings run out in December. Then he counted backward. To raise money he would need proof by September, which meant a paying customer by August, which meant a working prototype by June. Gurleen, sitting cross-legged with the laptop, asked, "And the logo?" "Does the logo help us get a paying customer by August?" "No." "Then not now." Every task got the same test: does this help prove something by September? The list on the wall shrank from twenty-two items to seven. It felt frightening and calm at the same time.

qa.q: How many months of savings did Gurpreet have?
qa.a: Gurpreet had savings for nine months.

qa.q: What does "frightening and calm at the same time" suggest about how Gurpreet feels?
qa.a: It suggests Gurpreet feels fear of the deadline but also comfort from having a clear plan.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do to keep to the timeline?
qa.a: Gurpreet could check progress against the dates every week and speak to possible customers early.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see the logo question and the answer?
qa.a: Gurleen may see it as a fair test that cuts distractions, and accepts putting the logo aside.

grounding: Gurpreet counts back from the last salary date to work out what must be proven by month six and judges every task against that date.

subtype: Approach: building a minimum viable version in six weeks [Action]
passage: Six weeks. That's what we gave ourselves. Himani and I sat in a borrowed room in Lucknow and built the ugliest invoicing tool you have ever seen, out of no-code tools and a spreadsheet. No custom backend, no login screen, nothing you would show in a pitch. I'm Gopika, by the way. At the end of week six we walked into twenty kirana shops with a phone, sat next to the shop owners and asked them to try it. Three said it was useless. Seven said they would pay if it printed in Hindi. One old shopkeeper pointed out that a button I would never have noticed was the wrong colour. We would have spent a year on the backend if we hadn't asked. Instead we spent our time fixing what people actually said.

qa.q: How many shop owners did Gopika and Himani show the tool to?
qa.a: They showed it to twenty shop owners.

qa.q: What does "the ugliest invoicing tool you have ever seen" suggest about how Gopika felt about showing it?
qa.a: It suggests Gopika felt a little embarrassed but was willing to show unfinished work anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could have worked instead of building a backend first?
qa.a: They could have asked shop owners about their invoicing habits first, or run the process by hand, because that also gets feedback before large work.

qa.q: How might the shop owners have felt being asked to try it?
qa.a: They may have felt listened to, since their comments about Hindi printing and the button colour were used.

grounding: Two founders build a bare-bones invoicing tool in six weeks with no-code tools and put it in front of twenty shop owners in Lucknow first.

subtype: Approach: polishing the product before showing anyone [Pitfall]
passage:
Month one, Monday. Sonali changed the app's button colour for the fourth time and told her friend Maria, "I can't show it yet. First impressions matter."

Month three, Wednesday. The icons had been redrawn twice. Maria asked, "Has anyone outside your laptop seen this?" "Not yet." Sonali checked the bank balance and told herself it was still fine.

Month five, Friday. The app looked beautiful. The bank balance showed three months of cash left. Nobody had ever touched the app. Sonali sat with the number and felt the floor go a little soft. "I was scared of looking amateur," she said to Maria. "So I made sure nobody saw it at all."

qa.q: How much cash did Sonali have left in month five?
qa.a: She had three months of cash left.

qa.q: What was Sonali afraid of?
qa.a: Sonali was afraid of looking amateur.

qa.q: What could Sonali do now with three months left?
qa.a: Sonali could show a rough version to a few real users this week and let their feedback decide what to improve.

qa.q: How might Maria have seen Sonali's approach over the months?
qa.a: Maria was probably worried, as the question about whether anyone outside the laptop had seen it suggests.

grounding: Sonali keeps polishing the app for months from fear of a weak first impression while cash drains and no customer feedback arrives.

subtype: Approach: weekly burn review with a kill threshold [Revision]
passage: I share a co-working table with two founders, Reena and Jagdish, and every Friday at five they close their laptops and open a notebook. One column for what they spent that week, one for sign-ups. I have watched this for months. In March the sign-ups grew but nobody paid. Reena had written a number at the top of the page and circled it: if the runway dropped under four months and still nobody paid, they would cut. In April it did. The next Monday they cancelled the paid design tool, thanked the freelancer, and started phoning shop owners themselves, one by one, phone on speaker. I could not tell what they felt. Jagdish looked flat for a couple of days. But by Friday there was a new entry in the sign-ups column, with a small tick beside it.

qa.q: What did the founders cut when cash fell below four months?
qa.a: They cancelled the paid design tool and thanked the freelancer.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have felt after the cuts, according to the narrator?
qa.a: The narrator cannot tell for sure, but Jagdish looked flat for a couple of days, so may have felt disappointed.

qa.q: What else could the founders do besides selling personally?
qa.a: They could ask the sign-ups why nobody pays, and adjust what they offer based on the answers.

qa.q: How does the narrator see the weekly review?
qa.a: The narrator sees it as disciplined, since the limit was set in advance and the decision was not made in panic.

grounding: The founders compare spending with sign-ups each Friday and, when cash falls below the set threshold with no paying user, cut costs and sell personally.
